answer: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality increased substantially for both white males and white females in the NLSY79 cohort (no sampling weights; each observation weighted equally). The shifted Gini coefficient rose from 0.255 to 0.464 for white males and from 0.080 to 0.429 for white females, and the P90/P50 ratio more than doubled in both groups (males: 13.8 → 37.5; females: 12.1 → 37.6). The increase was larger in absolute terms for females (Δ Gini +0.349 vs +0.208 for males), but this reflected a low 1990 baseline: in 1990, white females exhibited markedly lower wealth inequality than white males (Gini 0.08 vs 0.26). By 1996 the two groups had converged to nearly identical inequality levels (Gini ≈ 0.43–0.46; P90/P50 ≈ 37.5 for both), so the initial inter-sex inequality gap (Gini gap +0.18 in 1990) essentially closed (gap +0.03 in 1996). The rise in inequality was driven by a polarisation of the wealth distribution: the share of individuals with zero measurable wealth nearly doubled in both groups (males 25.7%→43.3%, females 20.3%→42.6%), the median fell (males $15,601→$8,900; females $20,100→$8,825), while the mean rose (males $88,163→$131,792; females $99,605→$128,837), indicating that aggregate wealth gains were concentrated at the top of the distribution. Complementary metrics (CV, mean-median gap, variance) corroborate the pattern, though CV declined slightly because the mean grew faster than the standard deviation.
